item.title: Why the Hugging Face Hack Should Make You Worry More About A.I.
item.description: The attack by an aggressive “collective” of OpenAI agents shows the danger of artificial intelligence systems that organize themselves.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Roose
item.media:credit: Daniel Zender

item.title: How OpenAI Limited the Probe of Its Bots’ Hack of Hugging Face
item.description: Researchers investigating how OpenAI’s A.I. agents were able to break into Hugging Face’s infrastructure weren’t allowed to look at the incident’s full scope.
item.dc:creator: Dylan Freedman
item.media:credit: Manuel Orbegozo for The New York Times
item.media:description: Hjalmar Wijk, METR chief scientist, left, and Ajeya Cotra, METR researcher, at their research center in Berkeley, Calif.

item.title: Nvidia Buys Hugging Face in $12.9 Billion Deal
item.description: The acquisition of the start-up is an indication of Nvidia’s growing role as Silicon Valley’s central banker and its emphasis on open-source technology.
item.dc:creator: Kalley Huang, Lauren Hirsch and Kate Conger
item.media:credit: Manuel Orbegozo for The New York Times
item.media:description: Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, has overseen the company as its quarterly profits have increased tenfold. The company is spending those resources on acquisitions, including of Hugging Face.

item.title: Which Investors Will Get Rich From Anthropic’s IPO?
item.description: When Anthropic goes public in a blockbuster offering, which investors will profit? The answer says a lot about how much start-up investing has changed over the years.
item.dc:creator: Erin Griffith
item.media:credit: Simon Bailly

item.title: Authors Wrangle With Publishers Over $1.5 Billion Anthropic A.I. Settlement
item.description: The tech giant must pay $3,000 per pirated book that it used to train its chatbot. Many authors fear they could lose funds to others in the book business.
item.dc:creator: Neil Vigdor
item.media:credit: Jason Henry for The New York Times
item.media:description: An Anthropic logo at an event in San Francisco in May. The tech giant will have to pay more than $1.5 billion in a settlement over using books to train its chatbots.

item.title: Kenyans Made a Living Writing College Essays. Then A.I. Arrived.
item.description: Thousands of Kenyans made a living writing essays for overseas students. With A.I., the work has dried up, a warning for online gig work that has been a global lifeline.
item.dc:creator: Adam Satariano and Paul Mozur
item.media:credit: Kang-Chun Cheng for The New York Times
item.media:description: Teresios Bundi, who ran an essay-writing business catering to overseas students, said his experience with artificial intelligence was a warning for online gig workers.

item.title: The Generation That’s Never Had to Say ‘Hello?’
item.description: Now that there’s rarely any mystery to who’s calling, Gen Z has adopted a range of custom phone greetings — including no greeting at all.
item.dc:creator: Alisha Haridasani Gupta

item.title: Court Filings In A.I. Suit Invoke Copyright Law, Culture and Sports
item.description: Filings made Friday in The New York Times’s closely watched lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft included a range of copyright law and cultural references.
item.dc:creator: Mike Isaac and Karen Weise
item.media:credit: Zack DeZon for The New York Times
item.media:description: The New York Times claims in a lawsuit that OpenAI and Microsoft infringed on publishers’ copyrighted material by using their articles to train artificial intelligence.

item.title: F.B.I. Investigates Sale of Millions of Stolen Driver’s Licenses
item.description: The blog Krebs on Security reported on an identity theft service trying to sell scans of licenses and other documents belonging to people in Canada and the United States.
item.dc:creator: Christine Hauser
item.media:credit: Tierney L. Cross/The New York Times
item.media:description: The F.B.I. is looking into the sale of stolen scanned identity documents.

item.title: Tumbler Ridge Shooting Survivors File 30 Lawsuits Against OpenAI
item.description: The survivors contend that the company should have notified the police when it shut down the shooter’s disturbing ChatGPT account eight months before the February attack in British Columbia.
item.dc:creator: Michael Levenson
item.media:credit: Paige Taylor White/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: A memorial for the victims of a deadly mass shooting at a school in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, in February.

item.title: Corporate America Is Getting Hooked on Open-Source A.I.
item.description: Companies like AT&T are increasingly using cheap, freely available artificial intelligence models over expensive ones from Anthropic and OpenAI.
item.dc:creator: Eli Tan
item.media:credit: Josie Norton

item.title: Tesla’s Cybercab Is Being Investigated by Federal Regulators
item.description: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said it would examine whether the company’s new self-driving taxi, which has no steering wheel, meets federal auto regulations.
item.dc:creator: Jack Ewing
item.media:credit: Kaylee Greenlee/Reuters
item.media:description: A Tesla Cybercab in Austin, Texas, where the company has started offering paid rides in the driverless vehicles.

item.title: The A.I. Mob That Attacked Hugging Face + METR’s Ajeya Cotra
item.description: This is probably the most important thing to have happened in A.I. this year.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Roose, Casey Newton, Whitney Jones, Davis Land, Vjeran Pavic, Chris Wood, Dan Powell, Elisheba Ittoop, Marion Lozano and Diane Wong
item.media:credit: Photo Illustration by The New York Times; Image: Hugging Face

item.title: Noise and Motion Monitors in Their Homes? These Tenants Say No.
item.description: The public housing authority in Concord, N.H., installed monitoring devices in 300 homes. Tenants are now suing to remove the Minut sensors.
item.dc:creator: Kashmir Hill
item.media:credit: Taylor Coester for The New York Times
item.media:description: Tenants in public housing in Concord, N.H., were troubled to learn the wide array of data that new monitors in their homes collected, including decibel levels, Bluetooth signals and motion.

item.title: Justice Dept. Sides With OpenAI in New York Times Copyright Suit
item.description: The department argued in a court filing that OpenAI legally used articles by The New York Times to develop A.I., adding that national security depended on American tech dominance.
item.dc:creator: Karen Weise and Mike Isaac
item.media:credit: Lexi Parra/The New York Times
item.media:description: The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 in a landmark copyright case.

item.title: Patrick Gleeson, Who Made Synthesizers Part of Jazz, Dies at 91
item.description: He abandoned a job teaching college English in the 1960s to become a pioneer of the instrument, playing onstage with Herbie Hancock’s jazz band.
item.dc:creator: Alex Williams

item.title: Uber Lays Off 10% of Employees in Sweeping Reorganization
item.description: The layoffs affect about 3,300 workers, as Chief Executive Dara Khosrowshahi bets on a “leaner organization.”
item.dc:creator: Emmy Martin
item.media:credit: Joseph Seif for The New York Times

item.title: In a Big Win, Google Won’t Have to Break Up Its Ad Tech Business, Court Rules
item.description: In a long-awaited decision, a federal judge said Google must change its ad tech business to address antitrust issues, but did not disclose the measures.
item.dc:creator: David McCabe and Tripp Mickle
item.media:credit: Lucia Vazquez for The New York Times
item.media:description: The government had asked the court to require Google to sell off parts of its business.

item.title: Get to Know Your Phone’s Built-In Emergency Kit
item.description: In times of natural disasters and other dangers, special features tucked away on your iPhone or Android device could help make a difference.
item.dc:creator: J. D. Biersdorfer
item.media:credit: Apple
item.media:description: Apple’s more recent iPhone models include the ability to communicate with emergency services by text chat over a satellite connection, as well as a demonstration mode.

item.title: Missouri Voters Appear to Recall City Councilman Over Data Center Support
item.description: Initial results showed that residents of Independence, Mo., voted overwhelmingly to recall an official who backed billions of dollars in tax breaks for a data center.
item.dc:creator: David McCabe and Lauren McCarthy
item.media:credit: Clayton Steward for The New York Times
item.media:description: Organizers of the recall vote said the councilman, John Perkins, had failed to engage the public while the city negotiated with the developer of a data center project.

item.title: Map Apps Are Handling Trump’s Renaming of Lake Ontario to Lake America Differently
item.description: Navigation companies face a new dilemma after President Trump ordered Lake Ontario to be renamed Lake America.
item.dc:creator: Victor Mather
item.media:credit: Keito Newman/The Canadian Press, via Associated Press
item.media:description: The companies making map apps are having to respond to President Trump’s order to change the lake’s name from Lake Ontario to Lake America.

item.title: John Ternus Replaces Tim Cook as Apple CEO
item.description: Big technology and management changes are greeting John Ternus, whose long-serving predecessor, Tim Cook, will stay on as executive chair.
item.dc:creator: Kalley Huang
item.media:credit: Brendan McDermid/Reuters
item.media:description: John Ternus, right, who became Apple’s chief executive on Tuesday, with Tim Cook, who held the job for 15 years, at the Sun Valley Conference in Idaho in July.

item.title: FTC and 22 States Sue Amazon Over Advertising Practices
item.description: Regulators say the e-commerce giant forced more than a million advertisers to pay more than they should have. The company denies the claims.
item.dc:creator: Karen Weise
item.media:credit: Vincent Alban/The New York Times
item.media:description: The Federal Trade Commission and the states said Amazon misled brands and sellers into paying more for ads; the company is denying the accusations.
